routes.description: Establish that consciousness, a persisting personal subject, future-directed purpose, objective value, and genuine agency contain features that no exhaustive physical description can constitute or explain.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least one motion-level feature is shown to be real and indispensable to personhood while remaining neither identical with nor fully explicable through physical structure, computation, function, or causal history.

motionBridge.description: Show that one or more essential features of persons require an ontological or explanatory basis beyond an exhaustive inventory of physical facts.

centralBridges.description: Establish that first-person experience is a determinate fact whose existence and qualitative character are not exhausted by neural, behavioral, or functional descriptions.
Establish that unified experience, memory, anticipation, reasoning, and choice require a continuing subject that uses but is not identical with the brain.
Establish that intentional purposes, objective values, and controlled alternative possibilities have normative or causal roles unavailable to purposeless physical processes alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support irreducibility by distinguishing the brain's provision of access to consciousness from the production or exhaustive constitution of consciousness.
Require justification for treating an unfinished and conceptually unsettled naturalistic program as capable of explaining every feature named in the motion.

routes.description: Show that consciousness and personhood arise through evolved physical organization while purpose, value, identity, and responsible agency remain genuine at appropriate functional and higher explanatory levels.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic accounts accommodate the phenomena named in the motion without eliminating their practical significance and no additional nonphysical subject, property, purpose giver, or causal power is required.

motionBridge.description: Show that materially realized processes and legitimate higher-level explanations jointly account for persons without implying metaphysical ingredients beyond the natural world.

centralBridges.description: Explain conscious perspective and the apparent self through unconscious brain computation, responsiveness, and an evolved user interface without positing a separate inner observer.
Explain how purposeless evolution, prediction, and socially developed practices generate genuine purposes and discoverable or improvable values without top-down design.
Establish that autonomy, self-control, reasoning, and robust abilities ground responsibility even if underlying processes are deterministic, while indeterminacy supplies no added control.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve indispensable personal-level explanations of meaning, love, beauty, and agency while denying that explanatory autonomy entails metaphysical irreducibility.
Ground confidence in further naturalistic explanation in its empirical record and explanatory economy rather than an unsupported promise of completeness.

sections.title: Consciousness and Physical Description
sections.rationale: Tests whether experience is ontologically basic or an additional fact beyond physical description, against accounts based on unconscious computation, neural responsiveness, functional capacities, and the rejection of an inner show.

sections.title: Personal Identity, the Self, and Continuity
sections.rationale: Addresses whether memory, anticipation, unified awareness, embodiment, and informational continuity require a persisting nonphysical subject or can be explained by an evolved self-model and materially realized organization.

sections.title: Purpose, Intentionality, and Future Direction
sections.rationale: Examines whether future-directed thought and action possess irreducible aboutness and causal efficacy or arise through natural selection, predictive processing, and organized goal-directed capacities.

sections.title: Value, Meaning, and Higher-Level Explanation
sections.rationale: Determines whether objective obligation, beauty, love, and meaningful conduct require realities beyond a physical catalogue or remain genuine through evolved practices and autonomous higher-level explanations.

sections.title: Freedom, Agency, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: Compares libertarian control by a deciding self with compatibilist autonomy and robust abilities, including whether alternative futures are required for culpability and whether indeterminacy adds control rather than randomness.

sections.title: Reduction, Causation, and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: Assesses substrate dependence, brain access versus production, causal and functional sufficiency, the conceptual boundary of the physical, and the evidential warrant for expecting naturalistic explanation to cover the full motion.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Consciousness is ontologically prior, while the material world is constructed from conscious experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Keith to define idealism, and the uninterrupted answer presents his first-person account.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly proposes idealism as a motion-level account, claiming consciousness exists in its own right and matter is constructed from it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: As a constructive move it clearly states the central ontological thesis, though its supporting inference remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but the sense in which matter is a logical construction from consciousness is only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A sweeping ontological conclusion is asserted from an idealist characterization without an argument excluding physicalist alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The position is internally intelligible, but the bridge from the priority of experience in presentation to ontological priority is undeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supplies an idealist model and historical illustration, but little evidence or comparative warrant for its universal ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The claim directly advances the pro motion bridge by placing consciousness ontologically before the material world.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own constructive position and does not materially interpret a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says consciousness exists in its own right and describes the material world as a construction from consciousness.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Scientific investigation indicates that conscious experience depends on complex unconscious computations in the brain, reversing the claim that experience is ontologically prior to the physical world.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Daniel for the naturalist account, and the ensuing sustained answer directly contrasts Keith's position.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether consciousness is ontologically prior rather than dependent on physical processes.

response.rationale: The reply directly counters priority by asserting that ordinary conscious experience depends on sophisticated unconscious brain computations, although dependence alone does not settle constitution.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the priority claim with a contrary dependence thesis, but leaves the dependence-to-ontology bridge implicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dependence claim is clear, though the scope of what scientific investigation has established about all experience is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Brain dependence is plausibly asserted, but treating it as undermining idealism requires a further metaphysical premise not made explicit.

charity.alternative: Idealism can accept systematic brain dependence as the structure through which consciousness is accessed or organized.
charity.decisiveQualification: Empirical dependence does not by itself establish that brain computation produces or exhaustively constitutes experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unconscious computational dependence to rejection of ontological priority is plausible but contains a material unstated bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to scientific investigation is relevant, but the excerpt gives no specific representative findings or comparison with idealist accommodation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro motion-level claim that consciousness is ontologically prior to the physical world.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately identifies experiential priority but gives limited attention to an idealist interpretation of neural dependence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says untutored waking experience depends on complex and sophisticated unconscious computations occurring in the brain.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Conscious awareness is an additional fact beyond any complete physical description because first-person experience remains directly known even while particular mental judgments can be fallible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator names Keith and requests his objection; Ward then gives a sustained first-person response about brains and awareness.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether neural computational dependence exhausts the fact of conscious awareness.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the computation account by distinguishing directly known awareness from physical description, but it does not explain why description cannot include or constitute that fact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the decisive explanatory issue but offers an asserted first-person remainder rather than a developed refutation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between fallible judgments and direct knowledge of being aware is clearly stated and appropriately qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges fallibility, but the move from direct awareness to being additional to every physical description remains somewhat overstated.

charity.alternative: A physicalist can accept direct first-person knowledge while identifying awareness with physically realized functional or neural states.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic directness and third-person descriptive difference do not alone entail ontological addition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The phenomenological premise is coherent, but the central inference from direct acquaintance to ontological addition remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person awareness supports the phenomenological premise, while the universal conclusion about physical descriptions lacks independent defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro bridge that first-person experience is not exhausted by physical description.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes brain talk but does not fully engage the strongest identity or realization account available to its opponent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes fallibility about particular contents from knowing that one is aware and calls awareness additional to physical description.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Positing consciousness beyond observable cognitive capacities repeats the discarded vitalist demand for an extra property beyond the processes that constitute life.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the moderator's request for a response, Dennett identifies Chalmers's formulation and argues against it in his own voice.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether an extra fact of consciousness remains after cognitive capacities are explained.
The broader idealist claim requires consciousness to be more than the capacities studied by cognitive science.

response.rationale: The vitalism analogy directly challenges the inference to an extra property, but resemblance to a discarded view does not establish that the consciousness case fails similarly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the extra-property demand explicitly, yet the analogy substitutes for a detailed comparison of the two explanatory gaps.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy is recoverable, but the alleged extra consciousness property and its relation to studied capacities are incompletely characterized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the position a repetition of vitalism carries more defeating force than the excerpt's limited structural analogy warrants.

charity.alternative: The hard-problem claimant can argue that phenomenal character differs categorically from vitalism's proposed biological force.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explaining behavioral capacities may leave the asserted first-person qualitative fact untouched.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy is intelligible, but the conclusion depends on an unsupported equivalence between biological function and phenomenal explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical analogy supplies suggestive precedent but no specific evidence that consciousness has the same explanatory status as vital force.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro consciousness bridge by denying the need for an extra conscious property.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially compresses the strongest distinction between phenomenal experience and the historical vitalist posit.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says Ward and Chalmers remake the vitalist mistake by positing consciousness beyond the capacities under study.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: The brain provides access to consciousness rather than producing it, so impaired neural retrieval need not establish that memories or consciousness have ceased to exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward begins with explicit disagreement and states his access model, including a clearly marked first-person conclusion about memory.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether brain dependence shows production or only mediated access to consciousness.

response.rationale: The access model directly offers an alternative interpretation of neural dependence, but the Alzheimer's example assumes rather than independently supports continuing inaccessible memories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the production inference, although its positive access account receives little mechanism or comparative support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The access-versus-production distinction and the Alzheimer's implication are clearly recoverable and openly presented as the speaker's view.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The continued existence of inaccessible memories is asserted confidently without evidence capable of distinguishing access failure from loss.

charity.alternative: Neural impairment may destroy or alter stored memory rather than merely block access to independently existing memories.
charity.decisiveQualification: Observed correlations do not uniquely select access, but neither do they establish persistence outside the impaired brain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The access model is logically possible, but the Alzheimer's conclusion relies on the very persistence thesis it is offered to support.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Neural impairment is compatible with access failure, yet no discriminating evidence supports memories continuing to exist beyond retrieval.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary pro access-not-production bridge and its intended distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The alternative production account is acknowledged only indirectly and its strongest evidential interpretation is not addressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt labels the brain an access machine and asserts that Alzheimer's blocks retrieval while the memories themselves continue to exist.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Memory, anticipation, and the ownership of experience require a persisting subject that is embodied and uses the brain but is not identical with it.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator asks Ward about the soul, Ward gives an extended account of the subject that possesses temporally linked experiences.

components.text: The earlier account requires explaining why unconscious brain computation cannot realize temporal ownership and continuity.
The extra-subject proposal also bears on the objection to positing entities beyond explained capacities.

response.rationale: The move provides issue-bearing contrary material about a persisting subject, but it does not directly show why computational or brain-based continuity cannot perform the ownership role.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It advances a relevant counterposition without contacting the decisive sufficiency premise of either earlier opposing account.

precisionFindings.rationale: A continuing owner of experience is clear, but what the subject is and how it uses yet differs from the brain remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity of a non-brain subject is asserted from temporal linkage without excluding materially realized continuity accounts.

charity.alternative: A temporally organized brain or self-model could own memories and anticipations without a separate persisting substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Functional continuity must explain ownership, but failure to stipulate a separate subject is not itself failure to do so.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The need for some bearer of experience is plausible, but the inference that it cannot be the brain is largely asserted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Memory and anticipation illustrate temporal unity, though they do not discriminate between nonphysical and brain-based subjects.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro bridge requiring a persisting agent subject distinct from the brain.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mentions the brain alternative but rejects it without addressing its strongest continuity-based formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that linked memories require a subject possessing experiences and explicitly rejects identifying that subject with the brain.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Consciousness and the apparent self function as an evolved user interface that simplifies internal and external complexity without requiring a separate inner user.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks who uses the brain, and Dennett immediately answers that the brain is its own user before developing the interface model.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether brain use requires a separate inner user or persisting non-brain subject.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the implied regress by saying the brain is its own user and consciousness is an evolved interface, though the excerpt only sketches the mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the separate-user demand with a functional alternative and states the defeating implication clearly.

precisionFindings.rationale: The interface model is clear, but calling consciousness a user illusion risks ambiguity between a useful model and unreal experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolutionary design plausibly explains simplification, while identifying consciousness wholesale with the interface exceeds the supplied support somewhat.

charity.alternative: The pro side can accept an interface while maintaining that a real subject experiences or uses it.
charity.decisiveQualification: A functional interface description must explain why no further experiencer is required, not merely omit one.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-interface account coherently avoids a separate inner observer, with one bounded bridge from function to exhaustive explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Computer-interface analogy and evolutionary utility support plausibility, but no detailed empirical mechanism or rival comparison is provided.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con bridge explaining self and conscious perspective without an inner observer.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the inner-user demand fairly but only briefly confronts the possibility of a subject underlying the interface.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes consciousness as an evolved and learned user interface that makes brains useful in guiding bodies through the world.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: A wholly physical account cannot preserve genuine purpose because physical laws and atomic processes have no purposes of their own, making experienced aims merely illusory.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly challenges the preceding naturalistic account and consistently presents Ward's first-person objection to physical causation.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether an evolved brain interface preserves genuine purposes rather than merely representing them.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that purposeless physical constituents cannot yield genuine purpose, but it assumes that wholes cannot possess functions absent from their parts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the genuine-purpose issue clearly, while leaving the crucial anti-emergence premise undefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear, but purpose shifts between intrinsic aims of atoms, system-level goals, and first-person intentions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that physicalism necessarily loses purpose is stronger than the premise that physical laws and atoms lack purposes.

charity.alternative: Purposes may be genuine higher-level organizational properties even when elementary laws and particles lack purposes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Emergence requires explanation, but absence at the component level does not entail absence in organized systems.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument relies on a composition principle that is neither stated nor defended and risks conflating levels of description.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Purposeless laws support the component premise but do not establish the claimed impossibility of organized system-level purpose.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con bridge that evolved physical organization can generate genuine purpose.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply treats naturalism as making purpose illusory and omits the strongest higher-level functional interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says atoms and physical laws have no purpose and concludes that a brain account makes experienced purposes part of an illusion.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Natural selection is a purposeless physical process that gradually creates genuine purposes in organisms, limbs, eyes, and tools without a top-down divine purpose giver.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly invokes Dennett's book and gives his characteristic Darwinian bottom-up explanation of purpose.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether a purposeless process can generate genuine system-level purposes.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects the component-to-whole inference by invoking natural selection as a bottom-up generator of biological and artifact functions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive impossibility claim and supplies a clear alternative generative account across several examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: Bottom-up emergence of purpose is stated consistently, with only the exact criterion separating genuine purpose from selected function left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident claim fits the familiar explanatory role of selection, while the metaphysical sufficiency claim remains modestly implicit.

charity.alternative: The pro objection can distinguish selected biological function from conscious, reason-guided, or intrinsic purpose.
charity.decisiveQualification: Natural selection explains functional directedness most directly and may not by itself explain every form of intentional purpose.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The bottom-up account coherently rebuts the composition assumption, with a bounded bridge from selected function to all genuine purpose.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Natural selection and the cited functions provide representative support, though the warrant extending this account to conscious aims is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con emergent-purpose bridge with a causal bottom-up explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly answers the general emergence objection but does not fully distinguish biological function from conscious intention.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies natural selection as purposeless yet purpose-generating and applies the account to organisms, limbs, eyes, and tools.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Future-directed intentionality resists physical reduction because a present idea can refer to a nonexistent future outcome and causally guide action toward realizing it.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person argument follows Ward's stated rejection of Dennett's project and develops his intentionality objection.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether selection-based functions explain present thoughts referring to and causing unrealized future outcomes.

response.rationale: The reply identifies future reference and causal guidance as phenomena needing explanation, but it mainly expresses difficulty rather than defeating predictive physical accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts an important unresolved component of purpose, though the challenge is posed more strongly than it is argued.

precisionFindings.rationale: The present-thought and future-outcome relation is clear, but the scope of the claimed failure of physical description is unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the point partly as a difficulty, but still moves too quickly from future nonexistence to physical inexplicability.

charity.alternative: A present neural representation can model a possible future and causally guide behavior without the future event acting backward.
charity.decisiveQualification: The causal work may be done by the present representation, while its semantic content still requires explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion trades on ambiguity between a future event causing behavior and a present representation being about that event.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary goal-directed action supports the phenomenon, but no evidence excludes present predictive representations in physical systems.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro bridge concerning intentional purposes and their causal role.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge overlooks the strongest representational account and risks treating the represented future as the physical cause.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how present behavior can be guided by a thought of a nonexistent future and says the idea appears causally effective.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Objective moral obligations are discovered rather than invented, and their connection to purpose and agency places value outside an exhaustive physical catalogue.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn uses Ward's first-person commitments and develops his linked account of value, agency, and the subject self.

response.rationale: This constructive move links discovered moral obligation, purpose, and agency to the claim that value is absent from an exhaustive physical catalogue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly states a motion-relevant value argument, although the bridge from objectivity to nonphysical ontology is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The moral realist thesis and catalogue claim are recoverable, though the intended sense of objective truth is not fully elaborated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Objective obligations and their exclusion from physical reality are asserted without resolving naturalistic moral realism or construction accounts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The value-purpose-agency linkage is coherent, but objective discoverability does not without further argument entail nonphysical status.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral phenomenology supports the discovery claim weakly, while no independent evidence or rival comparison establishes the ontological conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro purpose-value-freedom bridge through objective moral obligation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily constructs a moral-realist case and does not expressly interpret a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asserts obligations independent of belief, calls value absent from a physical catalogue, and connects value with purpose and agency.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Humanly constructed systems can contain discoverable constraints and opportunities for improvement, so evolved moral practices may support genuine moral discovery without requiring values external to nature.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly identifies Ward's position before answering through Darwinian predictive coding, chess, and cultural moral development.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether discovery and improvement require values to exist outside natural human practices.

response.rationale: The reply directly shows that construction and discovery are compatible, using chess to undercut the inference from moral discovery to external value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central discovery premise and supplies a clear counterexample, though morality-to-chess transfer needs qualification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The compatibility thesis is stable and clear; the respects in which moral codes resemble constructed games remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest compatibility conclusion is well fitted to the chess example and does not claim that the analogy proves a full metaethics.

charity.alternative: Objective moral obligations may constrain agents independently of any constructed practice in a way chess rules do not.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy defeats discovery-to-nonconstruction, but does not establish that morality actually is constructed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample validly shows that construction does not preclude discovery, with a bounded analogy gap concerning moral authority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Chess is a specific illustrative counterexample, though extrapolation to evolved morality lacks additional evidence and comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con bridge that evolved practices can sustain discoverable and improvable values.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly targets the stated inference while leaving the stronger practice-independent moral realist claim largely open.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says human constructs can contain surprises and discoveries, illustrating the claim through continuing discoveries within chess.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Responsibility-relevant freedom consists in autonomy, self-control, and robust practical abilities, none of which requires the underlying physical world to be indeterministic.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly presents the compatibilist view, using autonomous systems, self-control, and the putting example to define relevant freedom.

components.text: The earlier challenge asks how future-directed ideas can causally guide action within a physical description.

response.rationale: The move offers a relevant compatibilist account of freedom but does not answer the earlier intentional-causation challenge about present representations of future outcomes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is substantial contrary material on agency, yet it does not contact the decisive explanatory demand of its legal earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Freedom is expressly specified as autonomy, control, and practical capacity rather than metaphysical indeterminacy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is appropriately limited to responsibility-relevant freedoms and supported by a clear control distinction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The autonomy and heteronomy distinction coherently grounds a compatibilist conception of control with only bounded elaboration missing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The controller example supports the conceptual distinction, though broader responsibility claims lack detailed cases or empirical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con compatible-agency bridge by identifying freedom with autonomy and robust abilities.

representationalCharity.rationale: Within this selected span, the move develops its compatibilist position rather than interpreting a specific libertarian alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes autonomous systems from externally controlled systems and denies that ordinary freedoms depend on determinism being false.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom requires genuinely alternative futures under an agent's control, grounding culpability because the person need not have performed the wrongful act.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward identifies himself as a libertarian and develops the view through alternative futures, legal guilt, moral culpability, and Humean doubt.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether autonomy suffices without genuinely alternative futures controlled by the agent.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects compatibilist sufficiency by requiring controlled alternatives for culpability, but it largely stipulates that requirement rather than defending it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central freedom criterion and states a rival criterion, though its justificatory bridge is underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: Alternative futures and agent control are stable concepts here, though the relevant counterfactual conditions remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim has intuitive support but lacks argument against responsibility based on reasons-responsive capacities.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism grounds culpability in reasons-responsive control and robust abilities rather than identical-past alternative possibilities.
charity.decisiveQualification: A rewinding test may presuppose the disputed libertarian standard instead of refuting compatibilist control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The libertarian criterion is coherent, but its connection to culpability is asserted and risks begging the question against compatibilism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment clarifies the intuition, while no evidence or developed case establishes alternatives as necessary for responsibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con compatible-agency bridge by denying that deterministic autonomy is sufficient.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply states the opponent's rewind view but does not engage the strongest reasons-responsive account of responsibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says freedom requires an alternative set of futures and that it must be under the agent's control which future occurs.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: An agent self can decide among courses of action while upbringing, education, character, and habits influence choices without fully determining the decision made.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward contrasts deciding with merely finding oneself acting and explicitly identifies the subject self as an agent traditionally called the soul.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether influences on an autonomous person amount to determination or leave genuine agent choice.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes formative influences from determining conditions and locates the decision in the agent, but supplies no mechanism or independent criterion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the determinism issue clearly, though the asserted influence-determination distinction does most of the argumentative work.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between influence and determination is clear, and the speaker specifies education, character, and upbringing as influences.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that influences need not determine is plausible, but the stronger agent-causal implication is not independently warranted.

charity.alternative: A compatibilist can say the agent decides through character and reasons even when those conditions causally determine the decision.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling influences non-determining does not show that an additional agent-causal power operates.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is consistent but does not explain how an undetermined self selects a course without randomness or prior reasons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary decision language illustrates agency, but it does not distinguish libertarian causation from compatibilist decision processes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con agency bridge by asserting agent choice beyond determining physical and historical conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes formative conditions but does not confront the strongest view that those conditions constitute the deciding agent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says upbringing and education influence a person but do not determine the particular decision made at the moment of choice.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Adding genuine physical indeterminacy to an otherwise identical agent contributes randomness rather than greater control, trustworthiness, or responsibility.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett introduces the contrasting robot-babysitter thought experiment and draws the explicit conclusion that indeterminacy amounts to randomness.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether nondetermination adds agent control rather than merely introducing randomness.
The controlled-alternatives account requires explaining why an open future improves trustworthy agency.

response.rationale: The robot comparison diagnoses that substituting genuine randomness for determination adds unpredictability without a reason to prefer, trust, or credit the indeterminate agent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies the missing control bridge in libertarian indeterminacy and states the defeating consequence through a focused comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison clearly isolates indeterminacy while holding the agents otherwise fixed, making the intended control point recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The critique decisively targets bare randomness, though it does not exclude every sophisticated agent-causal account of indeterminacy.

charity.alternative: A libertarian may posit agent causation that controls indeterminate outcomes rather than a random event selecting them.
charity.decisiveQualification: The robot case defeats bare physical randomness but does not model an additional controlled agent-causal power.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The controlled comparison coherently shows that randomness alone supplies no added control, with a bounded scope limitation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment strongly supports the conceptual point, but it does not empirically or logically eliminate agent-causal models.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con agency bridge by denying that indeterminacy enhances responsibility or control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest agent-causal alternative remains live, although the reply fairly exposes the inadequacy of indeterminacy alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares otherwise similar robots differing only in genuine randomness and asks why anyone should entrust lives to the indeterminate one.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Reproducibility and practical immortality alter the force of promises, threats, and punishment, showing that ordinary moral personhood depends materially on mortality and vulnerability.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained argument uses Dennett's characteristic robot comparison and is immediately addressed by Ward as Dennett's preceding claim.

components.text: The earlier move's decisive demand concerns whether an agent chooses without being fully determined by formative influences.

response.rationale: The mortality discussion concerns conditions of ordinary moral personhood but does not answer how agent choice relates to determination and influence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies relevant higher-level material about responsibility, yet leaves the earlier causal-choice demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The point about fragility and contracts is visible, but the move shifts between robots, copies, immortality, and personhood.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Mortality plausibly affects incentives, but the categorical conclusion that robots are not people because they are not fragile is underwarranted.

charity.alternative: An immortal or reproducible agent might still understand promises, sanctions, attachment, and responsibility under altered practical conditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mortality changes stakes without necessarily constituting personhood or moral agency.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Possessing an informational encoding is insufficient for continued personal existence because stored structure must be concretely realized before the conscious or meaningful entity exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The Beethoven analogy advances Ward's recurring distinction between abstract information and an actually realized, experienced subject or work.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Purpose, beauty, joy, love, promising, mortality, and the desire for immortality can receive naturalistic explanations without losing their importance or wonder.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Naturalism remains an unfinished explanatory program, so confidence that it will ultimately describe every disputed feature of persons is a substantive commitment rather than an established result.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward poses a clearly adversarial follow-up that characterizes the acknowledged incompleteness of Dennett's naturalistic project as faith.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether asserted naturalistic adequacy is complete or remains a forward-looking research commitment.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
